Commentary
Heterozygote Deﬁciencies Caused by a
Wahlund Effect: Dispelling Unfounded
Expectations
GUHA DHARMARAJAN, 1 Department of Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, 47907, USA
WILLIAM S. BEATTY, Department of Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, 47907, USA
OLIN E. RHODES, Jr., 2,3 Department of Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, 47907, USA
ABSTRACT Population genetic tools can facilitate successful conservation and management of wildlife
populations. However, the ability of such approaches to inform wildlife management and conservation
programs depends upon assumptions linking genetic patterns to ecological processes, one implicit assumption
usually being that genetic parameters (e.g., population genetic differentiation) estimated using a set of loci
accurately reﬂect underlying demographic and microevolutionary forces affecting the population(s) under
study. This is an important assumption because it also implies that we have acknowledged that genetic
parameters estimated by a set of target loci inherently are associated with a sampling variance. Speciﬁcally, a
perception exists that heterozygote deﬁcits caused by biological mechanisms (e.g., a Wahlund effect) and null
alleles can be differentiated by the expectation that the former leads to a concordant pattern across all loci,
whereas the latter leads to locus-speciﬁc effects. We use Monte-Carlo simulation to demonstrate that these
expectations do not always hold under biologically realistic conditions. Our analyses indicate that the
conservative approach of discarding loci deviating from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium expectations could
rob us of our most informative markers, weakening our ability to interpret biological phenomena. ß 2012
The Wildlife Society.
KEY WORDS Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, heterozygote deficit, microsatellite, Monte-Carlo simulation, null allele,
Wahlund effect.
Molecular data in conjunction with population genetic anal-
yses are powerful tools that can be employed to facilitate the
conservation and management of wildlife species (Rhodes
and Smith 1992, Avise 1994: 361–398, Sunnucks 2000).
Population genetic approaches have been applied to elucidate
a wide variety of ecological processes at scales varying from
global (e.g., the effects of climate change; Hoffmann and
Willi 2008) to local (e.g., identiﬁcation of management units
and hybridization zones; Palsboll et al. [2007] and Latch and
Rhodes [2005], respectively). However, a fundamental but
often overlooked element of the successful development of
population genetics concepts for testing ecologically oriented
hypotheses is the satisfaction of assumptions that link genetic
expectations to ecological processes.
One of the most crucial assumptions implicitly made by
most population genetic studies is that genetic statistics
estimated from a set of target loci accurately reﬂect underly-
ing demographic and microevolutionary forces affecting the
population(s) under study. In reality, the underlying biolog-
ical processes (e.g., mating, dispersal) and/or study design
(e.g., number of individuals genotyped, the number of loci
used) critically affects the precision that can be achieved for
estimates of genetic parameters, ranging from those calcu-
lated for individual loci (e.g., Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
[HWE]) to those associated with greater levels of population
organization (e.g., population substructure, dispersal).
Failure to acknowledge the presence of such sampling vari-
ance can have critical consequences for the interpretation of
genetic parameters, especially when this sampling variance
inﬂuences assumptions that dictate whether individual loci
are suitable for inclusion in subsequent analyses.
One such set of assumptions, those associated with the
Hardy-Weinberg law, are central to deﬁning population
genetic expectations in diploid organisms (Crow 1999)
and the magnitude of deviation of observed genotypic fre-
quencies from HWE expectations is an inﬂuential parameter
estimated at individual loci (e.g., using Weir and
Cockerham’s [1984] estimator f ). In natural populations,
deviations from HWE expectations due to heterozygote
deﬁcits can be caused by biological factors related to mating
tactics (e.g., inbreeding), demography, and/or investigator
sampling (e.g., the Wahlund effect; see below). Alternatively,
heterozygote deﬁcits may also be caused by technical issues

related to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) ampliﬁcation of
genomic DNA (e.g., null alleles; Dakin and Avise 2004).
Because detection of null alleles are primarily based on tests
for heterozygote deﬁcits (e.g., Rousset and Raymond 1995,
Van Oosterhout et al. 2004), evaluating deviations from
HWE have become a mandatory ﬁrst step in population
genetic analyses, and consequently the results of these tests
determine which loci are included in subsequent analyses.
We address the relatively common practice of identifying
null alleles solely on HWE-based tests.
Dakin and Avise (2004) in their seminal review on the
occurrence of null alleles in microsatellite loci and the effects
of such null alleles on population genetic analyses (i.e.,
parentage) asserted that ‘‘proper multilocus analyses can
normally distinguish’’ between the heterozygote deﬁcits
caused by population genetic factors (e.g., Wahlund effect
or inbreeding) and those caused by null alleles because
‘‘population genetic factors should register more or less
concordantly across loci, whereas the effects of null alleles
are locus-speciﬁc.’’ This assertion (in various forms) has
since been repeated in other reviews (DeWoody et al.
2006, Selkoe and Toonen 2006) and either explicitly or
implicitly in numerous empirical studies (e.g., Iyengar
et al. 2005, Purcell et al. 2006, Olsen et al. 2008, Aguilar
and Jones 2009, Mayer et al. 2009). Although we do not
suggest that null alleles are not a potential cause for devia-
tions from HWE expectations, either in a general sense or in
the speciﬁc studies mentioned above, we emphasize that the
assertion of Dakin and Avise (2004) may not be upheld for
numerous reasons. As an example, we offer the case of cryptic
population genetic structure (e.g., demes, kin structure)
within a dataset.
The Wahlund effect refers to the reduction in observed
heterozygosity caused by (cryptic) population substructure
(Wahlund 1928). Mathematically, the effects of a Wahlund
effect can be demonstrated using Wright’s (1951) F-statis-
tics, which are related by the formula:
ð1  FITÞ ¼ ð1  FSTÞð1  FISÞ (1)
Thus, if an investigator unknowingly pools several subpo-
pulations that are genetically differentiated (i.e., FST > 0),
he/she will detect a deﬁcit of heterozygotes in the entire
sample (i.e., FIT > 0) even if each subpopulation is in HWE
(i.e., when FIS ¼ 0). However, inter-locus variance in FST
can be quite high because of many factors such as genetic
drift, migration rates, etc. (see Nei and Roychoudhury 1974,
Nei and Chakravarti 1977, Nei et al. 1977, Whitlock and
McCauley 1999). In addition, the power to detect signiﬁcant
genetic differentiation (i.e., FST > 0) also is affected by
locus-speciﬁc mutation rates and factors associated with
study design, such as the number of subpopulations sampled
and sample size (Waples and Gaggiotti 2006). Further, even
if all genotyped loci exhibit signiﬁcant FST , their ability to
detect a Wahlund effect (i.e., FIT > 0) may be compromised
for two reasons. First, even if random mating within sub-
populations occurs, they may be characterized by a hetero-
zygote excess (i.e., FIS < 0) if the effective population size is
small (Pudovkin et al. 1996, Luikart and Cornuet 1999). In
such situations, the power to detect cryptic population struc-
ture (i.e., a Wahlund effect) will be reduced because the
magnitude of FIT will be lesser than that of FST (equation 1).
Second, inter-locus variance in estimates of FIT is likely to
be large because it is not only inﬂuenced by factors affecting
variance in FST (see above) but also by those affecting
variance in FIS (e.g., family structure; Robertson and Hill
1984).
For the reasons cited above, and in contrast with the
assertion of Dakin and Avise (2004), a Wahlund effect is
likely to be associated with high inter-locus variance in FIT
(and the power to detect signiﬁcant heterozygote deﬁcits),
especially in the face of variable levels of polymorphism and
reduced sample size (see Rousset and Raymond 1995). The
failure to acknowledge both this variance among loci and the
stochastic effects of the sampling process is of concern,
speciﬁcally in regard to its consequences on the likelihood
of detecting deviations from HWE and concomitant deci-
sions pertaining to the retention of loci for subsequent
genetic investigations. We use simulated and empirical
data to demonstrate the ﬂaw in the assumption that devia-
tions from HWE caused by the presence of null alleles can
always be distinguished from those generated by alternative
biological mechanisms by evaluating the concordance of such
deviations across loci.
METHODS
Assuming the presence of cryptic population genetic struc-
ture (a population sample consisting of multiple demes), we
used R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna,
Austria) to carry out Monte-Carlo simulations to evaluate
the consequences of effective population size (NE ), migration
rate (M), number of demes (D), and sample size (S) on
several statistics of interest. The statistics evaluated include
the global means and inter-locus variances of Weir and
Cockerham’s (1984) estimators of FIS (f), F ST (u), and
FIT (F). We also calculated the proportion of loci that
revealed a signiﬁcant level of heterozygote deﬁcits in the
estimate of FIT (i.e., a statistical signature of a Wahlund
effect in the pooled population sample). We calculated the
statistical signiﬁcance of locus-speciﬁc FIT values as the
proportion of 1,000 randomizations of alleles among indi-
viduals that gave an estimate of FIT  the observed FIT
(following Goudet 1995). We calculated standard errors
for all statistics on the realizations of 250 independent
Monte-Carlo simulations. We brieﬂy describe the basic
structure of a single Monte-Carlo simulation below.
Individual-Based Monte-Carlo Simulations
For the purpose of Monte-Carlo simulations, we assumed
individuals to be characterized by a panel of 20 microsatel-
lites whose genotypes were determined by Mendelian segre-
gation of parental alleles. We assumed parental alleles
mutated at a locus-speciﬁc mutation rate (mLocus ) per gam-
ete/generation and new mutations gave rise to a new state
chosen from K ¼ 100 possible states (i.e., the K allele model;
Crow and Kimura 1970). We sampled the mLocus from a
Dharmarajan et al.  Wahlund Effect and Heterozygote Deficits 227
gamma distribution (m ¼ 0.001 and shape ¼ 1.33). We
chose the mean mutation rate as per Goudet et al. (2002),
and based the shape parameter on the average value reported
by Xu et al. (2005) for human microsatellite loci; sensitivity
analyses revealed that the shape parameter only had a small
effect on our results within biologically relevant limits
reported by Xu et al. (2005).
In each Monte-Carlo simulation, we assumed that the
global population was comprised of D demes, each with
an effective population size of NE individuals. We assumed
non-overlapping generations, and in each generation we
generated NE offspring (sex ratio ¼ 0.5) by the random
mating between adult males and females within each
deme. Reproduction occurred after dispersal, which followed
an island model assuming a migration rate of M. Thus, we
allowed NE M individuals from each deme to migrate with
equal probability to each of the D  1 remaining demes. We
allowed populations to evolve in silico for 1,000 generations
in each simulation; this number was sufﬁcient for observed
FST values to reach those expected under equilibrium con-
ditions using the formula for the n-island model (Slatkin
1985):

After the ﬁnal generation was completed, S individuals
were randomly selected from the global population (i.e.,
NE  D individuals) and all statistics of interest (i.e., global
means and inter-locus variances of the F-statistics and pro-
portion of loci revealing signiﬁcant heterozygote deﬁcits)
were estimated in this sample of individuals.
Simulation Parameters
Our simulations evaluated four major parameters of interest:
effective population size (NE ), migration rate (M), number of
demes (D), and sample size (S). To test for the effect of each
parameter, we ran simulations at ﬁve different values for NE
(50, 100, 250, 500, and 1,000 individuals), M (0.18  102 ,
0.36  102 , 0.9  102 , 1.8  102 , and 3.6  102 ), D
(2, 3, 4, 8, and 16 demes), and S (25, 50, 100, 250, and 500
individuals). Other than the speciﬁc parameter values that we
varied (see above), we ran simulations using the following
standard values: NE ¼ 250, M ¼ 0.9  102 , D ¼ 3, and
S ¼ 100 (FST-equib  0.05).
Empirical Data
We further tested if a Wahlund effect was characterized by a
consistent signature of heterozygote deﬁcits across loci using
an empirical dataset from raccoons (Procyon lotor). Raccoons
were trapped between April and June over 6 years (2003–
2008) in 35 spatially discrete habitat patches (local popula-
tions) located in the Upper Wabash River Basin, Indiana.
Raccoon trapping and handling methods conformed to
established ethical guidelines for use of wild mammals in
research (Gannon et al. 2007) and were approved by the
Purdue University Animal Care and Use Committee (pro-
tocol 01-079; for details see Dharmarajan et al. [2009] and
Beasley et al. [2011]). We employed genomic DNA
extracted from ear tissue to PCR amplify the microsatellites
using the protocols described by Fike et al. (2007) and we
achieved high quality genotypes using quality control meas-
ures standard in our laboratory (see Drauch et al. 2008). We
only used a subset of the raccoon genetic data described
above, which consisted of 653 individuals sampled from
16 local populations and genotyped at 12 microsatellite
loci. We chose these 12 loci because they exhibited no
signiﬁcant deviations from HWE at the scale of the local
population (Table 1) but revealed signiﬁcant levels
(P < 0.001) of FST among local populations. We selected
the local populations to ensure a minimum sample size of 25
individuals/local population. We used the genotypic data to
test for effects of pooling different numbers of populations
(2, 3, 4, 8, and 16 populations) and randomly sampling
different numbers of individuals (25, 50, 100, and 150)
from the pooled population on the proportion of loci reveal-
ing signiﬁcant levels of heterozygote deﬁcits in estimated FIT
(sample size constraints limited the combinations of the
above parameters that could be tested; see Results
Section). We calculated the statistical signiﬁcance of lo-
cus-speciﬁc FIT values using the randomization approach
described above for data from the Monte-Carlo simulations.
RESULTS
Our Monte-Carlo simulations were restricted to four major
parameters that could affect estimates of FIT, and these were:
effective population size (NE ), migration rate (M), number of
demes (D), and sample size (S). Three overall patterns were
clear from our simulations. First, our results indicated a
general heterozygote excess at the scale of the deme (i.e.,
FIS < 0) which led to the expected reduction in global
estimates of FIT versus FST (Fig. 1A–D). However, in the
parameter space considered, this heterozygote excess at the
scale of the deme had minimal effects on the power to detect
signiﬁcant heterozygote deﬁcits in the pooled sample. One
reason for this is that the parameter combinations that led to
the smallest global FIS (e.g., NE ¼ 50; Fig. 1A) were also the
